name: Nartheciaceae

lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach project Aletris as a basal-rosette monocot with a leafless scape, rough-textured 6-tepaled flowers in a raceme, 6 included stamens, a half-inferior 3-locular ovary and beaked capsule; explicitly reconcile older FNA broad-Liliaceae placement with current Nartheciaceae/Dioscoreales.

taxonomy_scope.historical_note: Flora of North America Vol. 26 describes Aletris under a broad Liliaceae treatment. Use that morphology but not that older family placement.

project_scope.note: Aletris aurea is accepted by current Kew and its native range extends through the southeastern U.S. to Texas.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start at ground level: a dense basal rosette of narrow leaves sends up a mostly leafless flowering scape. Then inspect the rough, mealy-looking 6-part flowers in the raceme.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Perennial rhizomatous/scapose herb with dense basal rosette of narrow leathery leaves.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers in a raceme, each with 6 tepals united basally into a campanulate/tubular perianth whose outside surface is rough or mealy. Six stamens are included and adnate to the perianth. Ovary is half-inferior and 3-locular; style branches near the apex.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Basal narrow-leaf rosette + leafless scape + rough 6-tepaled raceme + half-inferior ovary/beaked capsule = project Nartheciaceae/Aletris.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: basal rosette → scape/raceme → rough perianth → 6 stamens → half-inferior ovary → beaked capsule → Aletris aurea yellow flower → Joey Schoenocaulon comparison → taxonomy card
visual_lesson.intro: Aletris can resemble other spike-flowered monocots from a distance, so the learner needs two scales: whole-plant rosette/scape architecture and a close flower showing the rough perianth and half-inferior ovary.

steps.title: 1 · Separate rosette from scape
steps.look_for: Dense basal rosette of narrow leaves and a mostly leafless upright flower stalk.
steps.why_it_matters: Establishes the basic Aletris body plan.

steps.title: 2 · Touch the 'mealy' flower visually
steps.look_for: Campanulate yellow/golden flower whose outer perianth surface appears rough, grainy or farinose rather than smooth.
steps.why_it_matters: The rough perianth is a classic Aletris clue.

steps.title: 3 · Count six tepals and six stamens
steps.look_for: Six tepals united basally and six included stamens attached to the perianth.

steps.title: 4 · Show the half-inferior ovary
steps.look_for: Perianth tissue adnate to the lower part of a 3-locular ovary, leaving the upper ovary exposed.
steps.why_it_matters: A useful structural character that is otherwise easy to miss.

steps.title: 5 · Follow it to the beaked capsule
steps.look_for: Dry 3-locular capsule narrowing into a beak.

steps.title: 6 · Aletris aurea door
steps.look_for: Golden-yellow campanulate flowers about twice or less as long as broad, with erect lobes.
steps.why_it_matters: FNA separates A. aurea from yellow A. lutea by its shorter broader campanulate perianth.

steps.title: 7 · Compare with Joey's Schoenocaulon
steps.look_for: Both can present basal leaves plus an elongated flowering axis, but Schoenocaulon/Melanthiaceae shows a different open spike and flower/anther architecture; Aletris forms rough tubular/campanulate 6-tepaled flowers in a raceme.
steps.why_it_matters: Uses authoritative local monocot footage to prevent spike-form overgeneralization.

steps.title: 8 · Fix the family placement
steps.look_for: Older FNA broad Liliaceae treatment → current Nartheciaceae, order Dioscoreales.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents older morphology references from corrupting the current family backbone.

comparisons.title: Nartheciaceae/Aletris vs Melanthiaceae/Schoenocaulon
comparisons.rule: Aletris has a basal rosette and rough tubular/campanulate 6-tepaled flowers with a half-inferior ovary; Schoenocaulon has a different elongated spike and exposed flower/anther architecture. Use Joey's exact frames for the habit-level comparison.

comparisons.title: Nartheciaceae vs Smilacaceae
comparisons.rule: Aletris is a nonclimbing basal-rosette herb with a scape and capsule; Smilax is a tendrilled vine with broad reticulate leaves, separate-sex umbels and berries.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not copy FNA's older broad Liliaceae placement into the project taxonomy. Its Aletris morphology is useful, but the current backbone here follows Kew/APG: Nartheciaceae in Dioscoreales.

genera.fast_cue: basal rosette + leafless scape + rough 6-tepaled raceme + beaked capsule

taxonomy_reconciliation.note: Accepted by current Kew; native range extends to Texas.
Current Kew/APG placement is Nartheciaceae, order Dioscoreales.
